sections.content: If you're looking for real estate deals in Tulsa OK, you've landed on one of the most underrated investor markets in the entire country. While cities like Dallas and Phoenix grab the headlines, Tulsa quietly delivers strong returns — affordable entry prices, solid rent-to-price ratios, and a steady stream of distressed inventory. Whether you're wholesaling your first deal or building a rental portfolio, Tulsa deserves a serious look. If you're just getting started in this business, bookmark our [Real Estate Investing for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) guide before diving in — it covers the foundation you'll need to make smart moves in any market.
Tulsa OK Real Estate Market Overview

Tulsa is Oklahoma's second-largest city with a population of around 415,000 people and a metro area of nearly 1 million. The city has a diverse economy anchored by energy, aerospace, healthcare, and finance. Major employers include American Airlines Maintenance, ONEOK, Williams Companies, Saint Francis Health System, and Tulsa Public Schools. This economic diversity keeps unemployment relatively low and supports steady housing demand year-round.

The Tulsa real estate market sits well below the national average in home prices, making it accessible for investors who are priced out of coastal markets or even mid-sized Sun Belt cities. The cost of living in Tulsa is about 14% below the national average, which is a major reason why the city continues to attract remote workers and young families looking to stretch their dollars further.
Average Home Prices in Tulsa

As of 2024, the median home price in Tulsa proper sits around $175,000 to $195,000, though prices vary significantly by neighborhood. The metro-wide median is closer to $215,000. Distressed properties — the kind that attract wholesalers and flippers — can often be acquired in the $60,000 to $120,000 range, with after-repair values (ARV) landing between $130,000 and $220,000 depending on location and finishes. That spread creates real room for profit. Use our free [ARV Calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/arv-calculator) to quickly estimate what a renovated property could sell for in any Tulsa zip code.

Pro Tip: In Tulsa, the sweet spot for fix-and-flip deals tends to be homes with ARVs between $140,000 and $200,000. These properties attract the largest pool of buyers — first-time homeowners and move-up buyers — which means faster sales and fewer days on market after your renovation.
Best Neighborhoods for Real Estate Investors in Tulsa
Not every Tulsa ZIP code is created equal. Knowing where to focus your deal-finding efforts will save you time and money. Here's a breakdown of the most investor-friendly areas in the city right now.

North Tulsa is the highest-volume area for wholesale deals in the city. Home prices are low — often between $40,000 and $100,000 — and there is significant distressed inventory from aging homeowners, inherited properties, and pre-foreclosures. This area is best for experienced investors who understand how to manage renovation risk and price conservatively. ARVs typically land between $90,000 and $145,000.

Midtown is Tulsa's most desirable and stable area for investors. Neighborhoods like Brookside, Cherry Street, and Maple Ridge attract buyers and renters who are willing to pay a premium. Flip ARVs here frequently hit $200,000 to $350,000, and rental demand is consistently strong. Competition is stiffer in Midtown, but off-market deals still exist for investors willing to do the legwork.

East Tulsa offers a solid middle ground — moderate prices, decent ARVs, and strong rental demand from working-class families. Acquisition costs typically run $70,000 to $130,000 with ARVs landing between $140,000 and $185,000. This corridor is particularly good for building a buy-and-hold rental portfolio because vacancy rates are low and the tenant pool is large.
South Tulsa Suburbs (Broken Arrow, Jenks, Bixby)

The southern suburbs of the Tulsa metro — particularly Broken Arrow, Jenks, and Bixby — are fast-growing communities with excellent school systems. These areas are better for traditional flips and new construction than wholesale deals, as motivated sellers are harder to find. However, retail flips in these suburbs can yield $25,000 to $50,000 in net profit when executed well.
Types of Real Estate Deals Available in Tulsa
Wholesale Deals

Tulsa is one of the strongest wholesale markets in the South Central region. High volumes of aging housing stock, probate properties, and pre-foreclosures create a consistent pipeline of motivated sellers. Typical assignment fees in Tulsa range from $5,000 to $20,000 per deal, with North and East Tulsa generating the most volume. If you're new to wholesaling, read our [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) guide for a step-by-step breakdown of how to structure and close your first deal.
Fix and Flip

Flipping houses in Tulsa can be very profitable when you buy right. Average renovation costs for a Tulsa flip range from $20,000 to $55,000 depending on scope, and local contractor labor rates are lower than national averages. Midtown and East Tulsa are the best flip zones, where after-repair margins of 15% to 25% are achievable. The key is disciplined underwriting — always run your numbers through a tool like our free [Wholesale Deal Calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) before making any offer.
Rental Properties

Tulsa's rental market is one of the strongest arguments for buy-and-hold investing in this city. Average rents for single-family homes range from $850 to $1,400 per month depending on size and location. With acquisition prices as low as $90,000 to $130,000 in many parts of the city, investors can often achieve gross rent multipliers and cash-on-cash returns that are simply unavailable in larger markets. Vacancy rates citywide hover around 5%, and the strong University of Tulsa and OSU-Tulsa student populations add additional rental demand.
Tulsa Real Estate Market Trends to Watch

items: Population growth is steady but moderate — Tulsa is not a hyper-growth market, which means price appreciation is slower but also more sustainable for long-term investors.
Remote work migration continues to bring in buyers from higher cost-of-living cities, particularly from California, Colorado, and the Pacific Northwest.
Tulsa's 'Tulsa Remote' program, which offered $10,000 incentives to remote workers who relocated, has wound down but created lasting demand in the mid-price housing segment.
Inventory remains tight in Midtown and South Tulsa, putting upward pressure on prices in desirable areas.
Interest rate sensitivity: Because Tulsa prices are lower, the impact of rising mortgage rates is softer here than in expensive markets — buyers can still afford to purchase.
Distressed inventory is slowly increasing as pandemic-era forbearances have fully expired, creating new opportunities for wholesalers and flippers in 2024 and 2025.

sections.content: 'Tulsa is the kind of market that doesn't get on magazine covers, but it quietly makes investors wealthy. Low prices, low competition, and real cash flow — that's the formula.' — Common wisdom among veteran Oklahoma investors
Tips for Out-of-State Investors Targeting Tulsa

Tulsa is absolutely viable as a remote market, but out-of-state investors need to build the right local infrastructure before they start making offers. The good news is that Tulsa has an active investor community with plenty of experienced wholesalers, contractors, and property managers who work with remote buyers regularly. Here's how to approach the market from a distance.

items: Join the Tulsa Real Estate Investors Association (TREIA) — they host monthly meetings and it's one of the fastest ways to build a local network.
Find a boots-on-the-ground partner or acquisitions rep who can physically walk properties and assess condition before you commit to a deal.
Work with a local property manager from day one if you're buying rentals — look for managers who specialize in the specific neighborhoods where you're buying.
Use satellite tools and virtual tours to screen properties remotely, but always get a local inspection before closing on any acquisition.
Understand Tulsa's neighborhood boundaries carefully — a few blocks in the wrong direction can significantly change a property's value, rental demand, and risk profile.
Learn the local title companies and real estate attorneys who work with investors — Tulsa has several that specialize in wholesale and assignment transactions.

Study off-market deal sourcing strategies. The best Tulsa deals rarely hit the MLS. Check out our guide on [How to Find Off-Market Real Estate Deals](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/off-market-real-estate-deals) for proven methods that work in markets like Tulsa.

sections.content: Pro Tip: Before analyzing any specific deal in Tulsa, pull at least 10 comparable sales within a 0.5 mile radius in the last 90 days. Tulsa has enough micro-market variation that broader averages can be misleading. Tight comps are the foundation of accurate underwriting — learn more in our guide on [How to Analyze Real Estate Deals Like a Pro](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/how-to-analyze-real-estate-deals).
How to Start Finding Deals in Tulsa Right Now

The most consistent deal sources in Tulsa include direct mail campaigns to absentee owners and pre-foreclosures, driving for dollars in North and East Tulsa, probate court records, tax-delinquent property lists (available from the Tulsa County Treasurer's office), and networking with local wholesalers who have more deals than they can handle. Online platforms, auctions, and MLS-listed distressed properties round out the opportunity landscape. The Tulsa market rewards investors who are persistent and systematic about their deal-finding process.
